checks.prompt: A subtitling team uses the reference implementation of a well-known transcription model and has two complaints: processing their archive takes days, and their captions are visibly out of sync — words highlight a few hundred milliseconds late. Which of the two libraries addresses which complaint, and what is the underlying reason for the timing one?
checks.explanation: The two libraries solve different problems. One runs the identical checkpoints on a different inference engine — fused operators, batching, and quantised weights — for several times the throughput and much less memory, with accuracy unchanged because the weights are the same. The other is a pipeline on top that fixes timing, and the reason it can is important: the model's native timestamps are a guess emitted alongside the tokens, so they are thrown away and each word is re-timed by aligning the transcript to the audio with a separate phoneme recogniser.
options: The faster reimplementation addresses the speed complaint: the same weights on a different inference engine with operator fusion and quantisation, several times the throughput at a fraction of the memory. The pipeline library addresses the timing complaint, and the underlying reason is that the model's own timestamps are a by-product of token generation rather than a real alignment — the pipeline discards them and re-derives every word's start and end by force-aligning the transcript to the audio with a separate phoneme model
The faster reimplementation fixes both: quantisation makes the timestamps more precise as well as the run faster, and the pipeline library only adds speaker labels
The pipeline library fixes both, because batching the chunks is what produces both the speed-up and the tighter timing; the faster reimplementation is only a memory optimisation
Neither addresses the timing, which is inherent to the model; the only fix is a different model family

checks.prompt: Describe the relationship between the reference model, the faster reimplementation, and the pipeline built on top — as one brain with an engine swapped underneath and stages bolted on. Walk through the pipeline's stages in order. Then explain the three ideas the notebook says make it click, and be specific about which one is the biggest single lever on speed and memory.
checks.expected: A correct answer must establish the layering. The reference implementation is the correctness baseline: the same model weights, run in ordinary full-precision framework code, emitting only coarse per-segment timestamps. The faster reimplementation runs those SAME weights on a different inference engine, so accuracy is unchanged and only the runtime differs. The pipeline wraps that and adds stages. The stages must be given in order: voice-activity detection to find the speech, chunking, batched transcription through the fast engine, forced alignment of the transcript to the audio to obtain word-level timings, and optionally speaker diarisation, ending with words that each carry a start, an end and a speaker label. The three ideas must be stated. First, the fast library is a runtime swap rather than a better model — the accuracy is the checkpoint's. Second, detect speech first and transcribe only those regions, which both cuts the work and removes the silence over which such models famously invent text. Third, the pipeline's timestamps come from alignment rather than from the model, which is why they are tight. The biggest single lever must be identified as the precision or quantisation setting: dropping the weights to eight-bit integers is the largest speed and memory win, with an accuracy cost that is negligible on the largest checkpoint. A strong answer notes that neither library is a streaming solution — both are chunk and batch oriented — and that the pipeline's batching of the detected chunks is what lets it reach very high multiples of real time on an accelerator.

checks.prompt: A developer times their transcription call and reports that it returns in under a millisecond regardless of file length, so they conclude the model is not running. Separately they request half-precision on a machine with no accelerator and see no speed-up at all. What is happening in each case?
checks.explanation: Two quiet behaviours that mislead people in exactly this way. The transcription call hands back a lazy generator plus an information struct, so it returns immediately and the actual inference happens as you iterate — timing the call measures the setup and nothing else. And the precision setting is a request rather than a guarantee: a value the hardware cannot honour is silently downgraded, so asking for half precision on a machine without an accelerator quietly runs at full precision instead, which is why the effective setting is worth logging.
options: The transcription call returns a LAZY generator together with an information struct: nothing is computed until the segments are iterated, so timing the call itself measures nothing — materialise the generator if you need the work done up front. And a precision setting the hardware cannot honour is quietly downgraded rather than refused, so asking for half precision without an accelerator silently falls back to full precision; check the effective setting that was actually used
The instant return means the audio failed to decode and an empty result was produced; and the missing speed-up means the model was too small for quantisation to matter
The call is asynchronous and must be awaited; and half precision requires the pipeline library rather than the fast library
The instant return is caching from a previous run; and half precision is only applied when voice-activity detection is enabled

checks.prompt: Implement the stages the two libraries add. Write `frame_rms(samples, frame, hop)` returning the root-mean-square of each full window of `frame` samples taken every `hop` samples. Write `voiced_mask(rms, ratio=0.15)` returning, for each value, whether it exceeds the minimum plus `ratio` of the range (an empty input gives an empty list). Write `to_segments(mask, hop, sample_rate)` collapsing that boolean list into a list of `(start, end)` pairs in seconds, closing any run still open at the end. Write `merge_segments(segments, min_gap)` joining consecutive segments separated by less than `min_gap` seconds. Write `speech_fraction(segments, duration)` returning the summed segment length over the duration, raising `ValueError` for a non-positive duration. Write `align_words(segment)`, taking a dict with `start`, `end` and `text`: split the text on whitespace and return one dict per word with `word`, `start` and `end`, dividing the span in proportion to each word's character count so the entries are contiguous, the first starts exactly at the segment's start and the last ends exactly at its end; empty text gives an empty list. Write `assign_speakers(words, turns, unknown="UNKNOWN")`, where `turns` is a list of `(start, end, label)`: return NEW dicts, each the word plus a `speaker` key set to the label of the first turn whose half-open interval contains the word's midpoint, or `unknown` when none does. Write `lazy_transcribe(chunks, worker)` returning a generator that applies `worker` to each chunk, doing NOTHING until it is iterated. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Each block is one of the additions being modelled. The detection stage recovers the two spoken regions and shows the saving concretely: under half the audio ever reaches the model, and the part that does not is exactly the quiet stretch over which these models are prone to inventing text. The merging function is the counterweight — detection that is too eager fragments an utterance, and bridging short gaps is what stops a quiet word onset being cut off. The alignment block produces the structure that subtitle and highlighting code actually consumes: contiguous entries covering precisely the original span, with longer words occupying more of it. Speaker labels are then joined on by time, which is why the timing has to be right BEFORE diarisation can mean anything at all. And the last block is the one that catches people out in practice: building the result does no work, so timing the call measures nothing, and an unconsumed generator transcribes nothing at all.
checks.test:
SR = 16_000
FRAME, HOP = 400, 160

# Six seconds of quiet with two louder bursts in it.
samples = [0.01] * (6 * SR)
for start, end in ((0.5, 1.6), (3.4, 4.7)):
    for index in range(int(start * SR), int(end * SR)):
        samples[index] = 0.5

rms = frame_rms(samples, FRAME, HOP)
assert len(rms) == (len(samples) - FRAME) // HOP + 1
assert max(rms) > 10 * min(rms)

mask = voiced_mask(rms)
segments = to_segments(mask, HOP, SR)
assert len(segments) == 2, segments
assert abs(segments[0][0] - 0.5) < 0.05 and abs(segments[0][1] - 1.6) < 0.05, segments
assert abs(segments[1][0] - 3.4) < 0.05 and abs(segments[1][1] - 4.7) < 0.05, segments

# The saving is the whole point: only the speech is sent through the model, and the
# rest -- where a model is most likely to invent text -- is never seen.
fraction = speech_fraction(segments, 6.0)
assert 0.35 < fraction < 0.45, fraction
assert speech_fraction([], 6.0) == 0.0
assert speech_fraction([(0.0, 6.0)], 6.0) == 1.0
try:
    speech_fraction(segments, 0)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a non-positive duration must be refused")

# Detection that is too eager fragments one utterance into pieces; bridging short
# gaps is how a word onset stops being cut off.
choppy = [(0.0, 1.0), (1.05, 2.0), (5.0, 6.0)]
assert merge_segments(choppy, 0.2) == [(0.0, 2.0), (5.0, 6.0)]
assert merge_segments(choppy, 0.01) == choppy
assert merge_segments(choppy, 10.0) == [(0.0, 6.0)]
assert merge_segments([], 0.5) == []

# One coarse span becomes one entry per word, contiguous and covering exactly the
# same interval -- which is the structure subtitle and highlighting code consumes.
segment = {"start": 3.40, "end": 4.70, "text": "the quick brown fox jumps"}
words = align_words(segment)
assert [w["word"] for w in words] == ["the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps"]
assert words[0]["start"] == 3.40 and abs(words[-1]["end"] - 4.70) < 1e-12
for earlier, later in zip(words, words[1:]):
    assert abs(earlier["end"] - later["start"]) < 1e-12, (earlier, later)
    assert later["end"] > later["start"]
covered = sum(w["end"] - w["start"] for w in words)
assert abs(covered - (segment["end"] - segment["start"])) < 1e-9, covered
# A longer word occupies more of the span than a shorter one.
widths = {w["word"]: w["end"] - w["start"] for w in words}
assert widths["quick"] > widths["fox"], widths
assert abs(widths["fox"] - widths["the"]) < 1e-12, widths
assert align_words({"start": 0.0, "end": 1.0, "text": "   "}) == []

# Speaker labels are joined onto the words by time, which is why the timing has to
# be right BEFORE diarisation can mean anything.
turns = [(3.0, 4.0, "SPEAKER_00"), (4.0, 5.0, "SPEAKER_01")]
labelled = assign_speakers(words, turns)
assert all("speaker" in w for w in labelled)
assert labelled[0]["speaker"] == "SPEAKER_00", labelled[0]
assert labelled[-1]["speaker"] == "SPEAKER_01", labelled[-1]
assert {w["speaker"] for w in labelled} == {"SPEAKER_00", "SPEAKER_01"}
# A word falling outside every turn is labelled rather than dropped.
outside = assign_speakers([{"word": "hi", "start": 10.0, "end": 10.5}], turns)
assert outside[0]["speaker"] == "UNKNOWN", outside
# The original words are not modified in place.
assert "speaker" not in words[0]

# THE api gotcha: building the result does no work at all. Everything happens while
# you iterate, which is why timing the call tells you nothing.
done = []
result = lazy_transcribe(["a", "b", "c"], lambda chunk: done.append(chunk) or chunk.upper())
assert done == [], "nothing may run before iteration"
first = next(result)
assert first == "A" and done == ["a"], done
assert list(result) == ["B", "C"]
assert done == ["a", "b", "c"]

# Materialising it up front runs everything at once.
done.clear()
everything = list(lazy_transcribe(["x", "y"], lambda chunk: done.append(chunk) or chunk))
assert everything == ["x", "y"] and done == ["x", "y"]
done.clear()
lazy_transcribe(["x", "y"], lambda chunk: done.append(chunk))
assert done == [], "an unconsumed generator does nothing"

checks.prompt: A team ships word-timed subtitles and hits three problems: words at the start of quiet sentences are missing from the transcript; word timings for one language are as coarse as before; and the speaker-labelling step fails to download its model. What explains each?
checks.explanation: Three separate causes. Voice-activity detection is a trade: it suppresses invented text over silence, but set too aggressively it removes quiet word onsets, so its parameters are worth tuning when words disappear at segment edges. Forced alignment needs a phoneme model for the language in question, and where one does not exist the pipeline quietly falls back to the model's own coarse timestamps. And the speaker-labelling model is gated behind an access token and an acceptance of its terms, which is a setup step rather than a network failure — one reason that stage is heavier to adopt than the rest.
options: Aggressive voice-activity settings clip quiet word onsets, so the detection parameters — particularly how much silence must pass before a region is closed — need loosening. Word-level timing depends on a phoneme model existing for that language, and where none does the pipeline falls back to the coarse timestamps rather than erroring. And the speaker-labelling model is gated: it needs an access token and acceptance of its terms before it can be downloaded at all
The missing words mean the audio was not resampled; the coarse timings mean quantisation was too aggressive; and the download failure is a transient network problem to retry
All three are version coupling: pinning the libraries to matching releases restores the missing words, the fine timings and the download

The missing words are hallucination suppression working correctly and should be accepted; the coarse timings mean alignment was disabled; and the gated model can be replaced by any clustering algorithm with no setup

checks.prompt: Position the reference implementation, the faster reimplementation, the full pipeline, an on-device compiled port, and a managed cloud service. Say what each is for. Then advise a company that needs (a) a nightly batch transcribing thousands of hours on their own servers, and (b) live captions on a conference stream with under a second of delay. Say what you would use for each and be explicit about what neither of the first two libraries provides.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all five. The reference implementation is the correctness baseline and the canonical interface, but is the slowest, runs in full precision, and gives only coarse timestamps with no speaker information. The faster reimplementation is the production default for batch work: the same weights on a different inference engine, several times faster with much lower memory and built-in speech detection, at the cost of a converted model format and an interface whose results are lazily produced. The full pipeline adds word-accurate timing through forced alignment and speaker attribution, which is what subtitles, karaoke-style highlighting and meeting transcripts need, at the cost of extra dependencies, a gated speaker model and sensitivity to version pinning. The compiled on-device port is for edge and offline use with no runtime dependency on a scripting language and quantised weights, with fewer options and no built-in speaker attribution. The managed cloud service gives scale, real-time interfaces, built-in speaker attribution and service guarantees, at the cost of per-minute charges, audio leaving the machine and vendor lock-in. The advice must split the two jobs. The nightly batch on their own servers is the faster reimplementation's case exactly — throughput and memory are the constraints, speech detection cuts the work further, and the pipeline can be added if they also need word timing or speaker labels. The live captions requirement must be answered honestly: NEITHER library streams — both are chunk and batch oriented — so sub-second live captioning needs a genuinely streaming model or a managed real-time service. Noting that the fast library is not more accurate, only faster, since it runs the same weights, is a plus.
